Timeline::from_buffer¶

Back to Timeline API Reference

Signature¶

static Timeline Timeline::from_buffer(
    std::int64_t* data,
    std::span<const std::int64_t> sizes,
    std::span<const std::int64_t> strides,
    pluss::BlobDeleter deleter = {},
    std::string_view tz_name = "UTC")

Share Existing Storage With A Timeline¶

from_buffer() places Timeline semantics over an existing buffer of signed 64-bit UTC epoch-nanosecond ticks. It does not copy those ticks. The shape and element strides describe how logical positions map onto the buffer, while tz_name controls calendar interpretation and rendering.

This is the lowest-level Timeline constructor. Use it when another C++ component already owns a suitably aligned tick buffer, when a strided view must remain strided, or when copying a large temporal array would be wasteful. Use pluss::timeline::from_epoch() when values should instead be copied into storage managed entirely by Pluss.

Strides are measured in elements, not bytes. For sizes={2} and strides={2}, logical positions read data[0] and data[2]; data[1] is not part of the Timeline.

Ownership And Mutation¶

An empty deleter creates borrowed storage. The caller must keep the buffer alive, aligned, and unchanged in size until the Timeline and every copy or view derived from it have been destroyed.

A non-empty deleter transfers lifetime responsibility to shared Timeline storage. It is called once, with the original pointer, after the final owner is released. Copying the Timeline shares that ownership; it does not invoke the deleter early.

Because construction is zero-copy, writes through the original pointer are observable through the Timeline. Coordinate concurrent access yourself. The owning exports epoch_nanos(), ticks(), and copy_ticks() take snapshots instead.

Example: Own A Strided Allocation¶

#include <pluss/pluss.h>

#include <array>
#include <cstdlib>
#include <iostream>

int main() {
  bool released = false;
  {
    auto* raw = static_cast<std::int64_t*>(
        std::malloc(3 * sizeof(std::int64_t)));
    raw[0] = 0;
    raw[1] = 111;                 // padding, not a logical position
    raw[2] = 2'000'000'000LL;

    const std::array<std::int64_t, 1> sizes{2};
    const std::array<std::int64_t, 1> strides{2};
    const auto times = pluss::Timeline::from_buffer(
        raw, sizes, strides,
        [&](void* p) {
          released = true;
          std::free(p);
        },
        "UTC");

    std::cout << pluss::timeline::print(times) << '\n';
    std::cout << "released while Timeline lives: "
              << std::boolalpha << released << '\n';
  }
  std::cout << "released after Timeline dies: "
            << std::boolalpha << released << '\n';
}

Output¶

Timeline(shape=[2], tz=UTC)
[ 1970-01-01 00:00:00, 1970-01-01 00:00:02 ]
released while Timeline lives: false
released after Timeline dies: true

The output proves both contracts: logical traversal honors stride 2, and the callback runs only after the Timeline releases the allocation.

Contract And Failure Modes¶

  • data must address storage suitable for std::int64_t values.

  • sizes and strides must describe the same rank; Timeline supports ranks zero through three.

  • Every reachable offset must lie inside the allocation. The constructor cannot infer the allocation’s byte length and cannot prove that condition.

  • Timeline::kNaT is interpreted as the absent-instant sentinel. Every other bit pattern is an epoch-nanosecond tick.

  • tz_name does not reinterpret or shift the integers. It supplies the zone in which the same instants are rendered and decomposed into calendar fields.

  • A dangling borrowed buffer, an incorrect stride, or a deleter that does not match the allocation mechanism is a caller error with undefined behavior.
